scenarios.title: Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.domains: D1 Agentic Architecture · D2 Tool Design & MCP · D5 Context & Reliability
scenarios.brief: A meal-kit subscription company runs its support agent on the Claude Agent SDK. Its custom MCP tools are get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human and pause_subscription. The agent may refund up to $150 per box; larger refunds need a human. Eligibility checks go to a policy subagent through the Task tool. Most contacts are about missing or spoiled ingredients.

scenarios.title: Scenario 2 — Code Generation with Claude Code
scenarios.domains: D3 Claude Code Configuration & Workflows · D4 Prompt Engineering · D5 Context & Reliability
scenarios.brief: A clinic-scheduling startup uses Claude Code in one TypeScript repository: server/ (Node and Prisma), mobile/ (React Native) and packages/shared/ (types used by both). A committed .claude/ directory holds the team's commands and a root CLAUDE.md. Engineers use Claude Code to generate endpoints, screens and tests from tickets. Some also call it from small scripts.

questions.question: The agent's loop ends a turn whenever Claude's response contains a text block. Claude often writes a short line, such as “Let me check that box,” in the same response as a request to call lookup_order. In those chats the lookup never runs. The customer waits for an answer that never comes. Which change to the loop fixes this?

options.t: Set tool_choice to "any" on the first request after each customer message, then back to auto.
options.why: Runner-up. "any" is the right lever when Claude answers in text instead of requesting a tool. Here Claude did request the tool; the loop ended the turn before running it, and it would still do so.

options.t: Append each tool's output as a tool_result block carrying its tool_use_id before the next request.
options.why: Incorrect. Returning results correctly matters, but here the tool never ran, so there is no result to return.

options.t: Branch on the stop_reason of each response: run requested tools and loop on tool_use, stop on end_turn.
options.why: Correct. A response can hold text and a tool request together. stop_reason is the signal for what happens next: tool_use means run the tools and continue, end_turn means the turn is over.

options.t: End the turn only when the reply text has no pending-action phrase, and cap the loop at a fixed number of rounds.
options.why: Incorrect. Matching phrases in the text and using an iteration cap as the stop are both loop anti-patterns; the response already carries an explicit signal.

questions.decider: Claude did request the tool in the same response that held text; if Claude had answered in text with no tool request, forcing a call with tool_choice "any" would be the fix.
questions.explanation: Agentic loops branch on stop_reason, not on what the content looks like. One response can contain both a text block and a tool_use block; tool_use means execute and continue, end_turn means stop.

eli5.question: The loop stops as soon as Claude writes any words. The clue is: “in the same response as a request to call lookup_order.” Claude did ask for a tool; the loop just stopped listening.
eli5.answer: Picture a waiter who walks off the moment you say “hmm”, while you are still ordering. Every reply from Claude carries a label saying why it stopped (the stop_reason). tool_use means “run this tool and come back”; end_turn means “I'm done”. The loop should read the label, not guess from the words. Rule: continue on tool_use, finish on end_turn; never judge by the text.
options: Runner-up. Forcing a tool call (tool_choice "any") helps when Claude answers instead of asking for a tool. Here it asked; the loop stopped anyway.
Handing results back properly (tool_result blocks) is a later step. The tool never ran, so there is nothing to hand back.
Correct. Read the label: run tools on tool_use, stop on end_turn.
Guessing from the words, plus a round limit, is still guessing. The reply already says why it stopped.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a response is either words or a tool call, so any text means Claude has finished. It isn't. One response can hold a text block and a tool_use block. The official signal for what to do next is stop_reason, not the shape of the content.
deep.diagram:
one response
 ├ content: [text "Let me check", tool_use]
 └ stop_reason: tool_use   ← this decides
 tool_use → run tools, send results, loop
 end_turn → finished

evidence.means: The loop decides by looking at content. The guide names this anti-pattern: checking assistant text as a completion signal.

guide.obj: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops
guide.quote: Continue the loop when stop_reason == "tool_use"; terminate when "end_turn".

questions.question: The coordinator sends eligibility questions to the policy subagent with the Task tool. Its prompt reads: “Check whether this customer's claim is eligible.” The subagent's verdicts are generic and often hedge. The facts it needs are only in the chat: which items spoiled, when the box arrived, and what the customer wants. Which change best improves the verdicts?

options.t: Have the coordinator restate the case, with products, arrival day and desired remedy, in its Task call.
options.why: Correct. Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history. Whatever the subagent needs must be written into the prompt it receives.

options.t: Give the policy subagent read-only get_customer and lookup_order and let it gather the case itself.
options.why: Runner-up. Scoped lookup tools are right when the facts live in backend records. Which items spoiled and what the customer wants exist only in the chat, and no tool returns them.

options.t: Add the eligibility policy and two worked verdicts to the subagent's AgentDefinition system prompt.
options.why: Incorrect. Better instructions and examples improve how the subagent reasons, but it still lacks this case's facts.

options.t: Have the subagent return a structured verdict listing eligibility, the reason and any facts it still needs.
options.why: Incorrect. Asking back for missing facts adds a round trip for every claim; the coordinator already has the facts and can send them.

questions.decider: The needed facts exist only in the chat, which the subagent cannot see; if they lived in backend records, scoped lookup tools for the subagent could compete.
questions.explanation: Subagents start with isolated context: they see only the prompt the coordinator writes. Facts that exist only in the conversation must be passed explicitly in the Task prompt.

eli5.question: A helper (the policy subagent) gives vague answers. The clue is: “The facts it needs are only in the chat.” The helper never sees the chat.
eli5.answer: It is like asking a colleague in another office “is this claim OK?” without sending the claim. They can only guess. A subagent starts with a blank page; it does not see the coordinator's conversation. So the coordinator must write the facts into the request (the Task prompt). Rule: a subagent knows only what you put in its prompt.
options: Correct. Send the facts with the question.
Runner-up. Letting the helper look things up works when the facts are in a database. These are in the customer's own words, which no tool returns.
Teaching the helper the policy with examples doesn't tell it what happened in this case.
Letting the helper ask for what's missing works, but costs a round trip every time when the facts could be sent up front.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a subagent can see what the coordinator saw, so a short question is enough. It can't. Subagents have isolated context: no shared memory, no inherited history. A one-line Task prompt gives the subagent one line of information.
deep.diagram:
coordinator context: chat + tool results
        │ Task(prompt)  ← the only bridge
        ▼
subagent context: prompt only

guide.obj: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
guide.quote: Subagent context must be provided explicitly in the prompt (no automatic inheritance / shared memory).

questions.question: Cancellations are handled by people, so the agent routes them through escalate_to_human. Product wants the agent to offer a pause before it escalates a cancellation. This is a retention nudge, not a policy. Missing it in some chats is acceptable. The change should be light to maintain. Which TWO changes fit best?

options.t: Force pause_subscription through tool_choice on the turn where a customer first asks to cancel.
options.why: Incorrect. Forcing the tool pauses the subscription without the customer agreeing. The goal is to offer a pause, not to apply one.

options.t: Add a system-prompt instruction to suggest pausing deliveries before routing a cancellation request to a person.
options.why: Correct. A soft goal where occasional misses are fine is exactly what prompt guidance is for. It is one line to maintain.

options.t: Add a PreToolUse hook that denies escalate_to_human on cancellations until a pause has been offered.
options.why: Runner-up. A hook is the right tool when a step must happen every time. Here misses are acceptable, so code that must detect cancellations and offers is more machinery than the goal needs.

options.t: Include two or three sample chats where the agent suggests a pause and then escalates once the customer declines.
options.why: Correct. A few examples show the order of steps and the tone, and make the nudge consistent without any code.

questions.decider: Missing the offer in some chats is acceptable; if it had to happen in every cancellation, a hook would beat prompt guidance.
questions.explanation: Programmatic enforcement is for steps that must happen every time. A soft, best-effort behaviour is best shaped with a clear instruction plus a few examples.

eli5.question: Product wants a friendly “would you like to pause instead?” before cancellations go to a person. The clue is: “Missing it in some chats is acceptable.” That makes it a nudge, not a rule.
eli5.answer: A shop asks staff to mention the loyalty card at the till. A reminder note and a short demo do the job; nobody installs a till that locks until the card is mentioned. Here, an instruction in the system prompt plus a few example chats is enough. Rule: must-happen-every-time → code; nice-to-have → prompt and examples.
options: Forcing the pause tool would pause people who only wanted to talk about cancelling.
Correct. A plain instruction sets the nudge.
Runner-up. A guard in code (a PreToolUse hook) is for steps that must never be skipped. Here skipping is allowed.
Correct. Examples show exactly how the offer and the hand-off should sound.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think code is the more professional answer whenever behaviour must change. The guide's line is narrower: code (hooks, gates) is for deterministic compliance, where a single miss is a failure. When misses are acceptable, a hook adds logic to maintain and a way to block legitimate escalations.

evidence.quote: This is a retention nudge, not a policy.
evidence.means: Nothing breaks if it is skipped.

evidence.quote: Missing it in some chats is acceptable.
evidence.means: The decider. Deterministic enforcement ([[2]]) solves a requirement nobody has.

evidence.quote: The change should be light to maintain.
evidence.means: An instruction ([[1]]) and a few examples ([[3]]) are the lightest pair that works.

deep.rule: Code for must-always; prompt and examples for should-usually.

guide.obj: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
guide.quote: When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial ops), prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate.

questions.question: get_customer returns the full card number on file, because the billing team's tools need it. That team owns the server and will not change it. Twice, the support agent read a card number back to a customer. Security says a card number must not reach a customer in any chat. Which change meets this requirement?

options.t: Add a system-prompt rule to refer to cards by their last four digits only, with two example replies to copy.
options.why: Runner-up. A clear rule with examples is the right fix for a should-usually behaviour. Security needs a must-never, and prompt compliance has a non-zero failure rate.

options.t: Register a PostToolUse hook that masks the card field in each get_customer result before Claude reads it.
options.why: Correct. The hook rewrites the result before the model sees it, so the agent cannot repeat a number it never had. It needs no change to the billing team's server.

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that logs any card number found in a tool result for security to review.
options.why: Incorrect. Right hook, wrong action: logging records exposure after the model has the number; it does not stop the number reaching a reply.

options.t: Route get_customer through a subagent whose definition returns only name, plan and box IDs.
options.why: Incorrect. The subagent still receives the full number and decides what to pass on; its definition is an instruction, not a filter.

questions.decider: The rule is “must not reach a customer in any chat” and the server cannot change; if the goal were only to reduce leaks, a prompt rule with an example could do.
questions.explanation: When a tool returns data the model must never use, transform the result with a PostToolUse hook before the model sees it. Prompt rules only make misuse less likely.

eli5.question: The agent sometimes reads out a customer's card number. The clue is: “a card number must not reach a customer in any chat.” That is a must-never.
eli5.answer: If you do not want a receptionist reading out card numbers, do not hand them the number: black it out on the paper first. A PostToolUse hook is that black marker. It edits each tool result before Claude reads it. Claude cannot repeat what it never saw. Rule: if the model must never use some data, remove it before the model sees it.
options: Runner-up. A written rule with examples usually works, but “usually” is not enough for a must-never.
Correct. Mask the number before Claude ever sees it.
A hook that only writes a log entry notices the number but still hands it to Claude.
A helper told to pass on only some fields still sees the number, and might pass it on.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a firm instruction stops the model saying something. It lowers the chance, but prompt compliance is probabilistic. For data that must never reach a customer, the reliable layer is the tool result itself: change it before the model reads it.
deep.diagram:
get_customer → [PostToolUse hook: mask card] → Claude
 server unchanged        model never sees full number

questions.question: After each chat, a wrap-up request asks Claude to log the outcome. It should call one of three tools: record_resolved, record_escalated or record_abandoned. Each feeds a queue another team owns, so they cannot be merged. Claude picks the right tool when it calls one. Sometimes it replies with a text summary instead. Which change fits best?

options.t: Merge the three into one record_outcome tool with an outcome enum, forced by name in tool_choice.
options.why: Runner-up. Forcing one named tool is the cleanest guarantee when a single tool fits. The tools feed separate queues and cannot be merged, so this is not available.

options.t: Keep tool_choice on auto and add a when-to-use line and an example to each record tool's description.
options.why: Incorrect. Better descriptions improve which tool is picked, and selection already works; with auto, Claude can still reply in text.

options.t: Check stop_reason on the wrap-up reply and resend with a reminder line whenever it comes back as end_turn.
options.why: Incorrect. Detecting the miss and resending lowers the failure rate at the cost of extra calls; the API can require a tool call in the first place.

options.t: Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} on the wrap-up request only, keeping auto for the chat.
options.why: Correct. "any" requires a tool call while still letting Claude choose which one, and its choices are already right.

questions.decider: Claude must choose among three tools that cannot be merged; if a single tool were always the right one, forcing it by name would win.
questions.explanation: tool_choice "auto" allows text; "any" requires some tool call; a forced tool requires a specific one. When the model must pick among several tools but must not answer in text, use "any".

eli5.question: Claude sometimes writes a note instead of filling in one of three forms. The clue is: Claude “picks the right tool when it calls one”, and the three tools “cannot be merged.”
eli5.answer: Think of a clerk who must stamp a file with one of three stamps. Sometimes they write a sticky note instead. You don't tape one stamp to their hand; you say “you must use a stamp, your choice which.” That is tool_choice: "any": some tool must be called, and Claude picks which. Rule: one specific tool → force it by name; must pick among several → "any".
options: Runner-up. Forcing one named tool is perfect when there is only one right tool. Here the three can't be merged into one.
Clearer tool labels help Claude pick the right tool. It already does; the problem is it sometimes picks none.
Catching the miss and asking again works most of the time, but costs calls and still isn't certain.
Correct. A tool call is required; Claude still chooses which.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think “force a tool” is the only way to stop text replies. There are two forcing modes. A named tool forces which tool; "any" forces that a tool is called but leaves the choice to Claude. When the choice is already right, keep it and only remove the text option.
deep.diagram:
auto   → text OR any tool
any    → some tool (Claude picks)
forced → this one named tool

guide.quote: "any" guarantees a tool call rather than text

questions.question: lookup_order takes a box ID, and its whole description reads “Looks up a box”. Customers usually name a box by when it came, such as “last Tuesday's box”. The agent then passes that date as the box ID, and the call fails. Each customer's box IDs are listed in the get_customer record. What is the most effective first step?

options.t: Expand the description with the ID format, a sample call, and how to go from a date to an ID.
options.why: Correct. Descriptions are the main way the model learns how to call a tool. This one gives no input format and no route from a date to an ID, and fixing that is cheap.

options.t: Return a structured validation error from lookup_order that names the expected ID format and an example.
options.why: Incorrect. A clear validation error helps the agent recover after a bad call. The first step is to stop the bad call.

options.t: Add a few-shot example to the system prompt that resolves a date-based request through get_customer first.
options.why: Runner-up. Examples help once the descriptions are clear but behaviour is still inconsistent. With a one-line description, the root cause is the description, and examples add tokens without fixing it.

options.t: Add a lookup_order_by_date tool that accepts a delivery date and returns the customer's matching box.
options.why: Incorrect. A new tool is more work than a first step, and with minimal descriptions the agent may misuse it too.

questions.decider: The description is one line with no input format; if it already listed formats and examples and the misuse continued, examples or a validation error would come next.
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary signal for how to call a tool. A minimal description should first be expanded with input format, examples, edge cases and boundaries.

eli5.question: The agent passes a date where an ID belongs. The clue is: its whole description reads “Looks up a box.” Nobody told the agent what to pass in.
eli5.answer: A form with a box that just says “Box” gets filled with all sorts of things. Write “Box ID, like BX-1234; find it on the customer's record” and people fill it right. The tool description is that label. Fix it first: it is cheap and goes at the root. Rule: a tool is called the way its description explains it; start there.
options: Correct. Say what the input looks like and how to get it from a date.
A helpful error message helps after the mistake. Better to prevent the mistake.
Runner-up. Example chats (few-shot) help once the label is clear. With a one-line label, fix the label first.
A whole new tool is a bigger job than a first step.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think misuse is a reasoning problem that examples or error messages should fix. Usually it is an information problem. The model decides how to call a tool mainly from its description. A one-line description gives no input format, no examples and no boundaries.

questions.question: pause_subscription fails when the next box is past its packing cut-off. The cut-off varies by delivery region, and only the backend knows it. Today the tool returns isError with the text “Request failed.” The agent retries several times, then tells the customer the system is down. Which change is best?

options.t: Describe the packing cut-off in the tool description and tell the agent to check the box date before calling.
options.why: Runner-up. Putting a rule in the description works when the agent can check it in advance. The cut-off varies by region and only the backend knows it, so the agent cannot check it.

options.t: Return errorCategory “transient” with isRetryable false and the text “Pause unavailable for this box.”
options.why: Incorrect. Structured, but mislabelled and empty: transient says outage, and the agent still has nothing true to tell the customer.

options.t: Return errorCategory “business” with isRetryable false, the region's cut-off and the next pausable box.
options.why: Correct. The failure is a policy outcome, not an outage. A business category with a retryable flag of false stops the retries, and the note gives the agent something true to tell the customer.

options.t: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks repeat pause_subscription calls and tells the agent to escalate.
options.why: Incorrect. This stops the retries but sends a policy outcome the agent could explain to a human, and still gives no reason.

questions.decider: Only the backend knows the region's cut-off, so the agent learns it only from the error; if the cut-off were fixed and known in advance, describing it in the tool description could prevent the call.
questions.explanation: A generic failure gives the agent no basis for recovery. Business-rule failures should carry a category, a not-retryable flag and a customer-friendly explanation.

eli5.question: The pause fails because the box is already being packed, but the tool only says “Request failed.” The clue is: “only the backend knows it.” The agent can't know the cut-off in advance.
eli5.answer: If a shop till just beeps “error”, the cashier tries again and again. If it says “too late, this order already left; next one can be changed”, the cashier explains it and moves on. A structured error with a category, “don't retry”, and a plain note does that. Rule: say what kind of failure it is and whether retrying can help.
options: Runner-up. Explaining the rule up front works when the agent can check it. Here only the backend knows the cut-off.
A labelled error helps, but this label says “outage” and gives no reason the customer can understand.
Correct. Name it a rule outcome, say don't retry, and give a sentence to pass on.
Blocking repeats and escalating stops the loop, but a person gets a case the agent could have explained itself.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think repeated retries are the bug to fix. They are a symptom. The agent retries because “Request failed” looks like an outage. Give it the kind of failure and whether retrying can help, and the retries and the wrong message both go away.

evidence.quote: The cut-off varies by delivery region, and only the backend knows it.
evidence.means: The decider: the agent can't check this beforehand, so describing it ([[0]]) won't prevent the call.

evidence.quote: Today the tool returns isError with the text “Request failed.”

evidence.quote: The agent retries several times, then tells the customer the system is down.

guide.obj: 2.2 Implement structured error responses for MCP tools
guide.quote: retriable: false + customer-friendly explanation for business violations

questions.question: A customer writes: “My salmon was missing again. I want to speak to a real person.” The refund is well inside the agent's limit, so it could settle the case alone. The customer sounds calm. The request for a person is direct and unambiguous. How should the agent respond?

options.t: Acknowledge the problem, offer the refund it can issue now, and escalate if the customer asks for a person again.
options.why: Runner-up. Offering a resolution first is right when a customer is frustrated but has not asked for a person. Here the request is direct, so the agent should not make the customer ask twice.

options.t: Run lookup_order to confirm the missing item first, then decide between refunding and escalating.
options.why: Incorrect. Investigating before honouring an explicit request delays the customer for a decision that is already made.

options.t: Check the customer's refund history first, and escalate only if the item has gone missing on an earlier box too.
options.why: Incorrect. Repeat issues can matter for policy, but the customer asked for a person; that trigger does not depend on history.

options.t: Call escalate_to_human straight away, with the customer ID, the box and the missing item in the handoff.
options.why: Correct. An explicit request for a human is an escalation trigger on its own. Honour it immediately and pass the facts so the person can pick up without re-asking.

questions.decider: The customer explicitly asks for a person; if they were only frustrated without asking, offering the in-limit refund first would be right.
questions.explanation: Escalation triggers include an explicit request for a human, policy gaps and inability to progress. Explicit requests are honoured immediately, with a handoff summary.

questions.obj: 5.3 Access failure vs valid empty result
questions.question: The policy subagent checks a customer's past refunds through a payments API. When that API times out, the subagent tells the coordinator “No previous refunds found.” The coordinator then approves refunds that repeat earlier ones. The API's outages usually last about an hour. How should the subagent report this case?

options.t: Retry with backoff inside the subagent, then report “history unavailable” to the coordinator if every retry fails.
options.why: Runner-up. Local recovery first is good practice for brief blips. With hour-long outages the retries run out, and a bare “unavailable” status hides what was tried and what was retrieved.

options.t: Report the timeout as a failed lookup, naming the query it tried and any past refunds it did retrieve.
options.why: Correct. An access failure must look different from a valid empty result. With the failure type, the query and partial results, the coordinator can hold the refund, escalate or try later.

options.t: Return isError with errorCategory “transient” and let the coordinator rerun the subagent later.
options.why: Incorrect. This separates failure from empty, which is half the fix, but drops the attempted query and any partial results the coordinator could act on now.

options.t: Have the coordinator call the payments API itself and skip the subagent for refund-history checks.
options.why: Incorrect. Moving the call does not fix how a timeout is reported; the coordinator would face the same ambiguity.

questions.decider: Outages last about an hour, so retries alone fail and the report itself must distinguish failure from empty; if timeouts were brief blips, local retry would come first.
questions.explanation: A timeout reported as “nothing found” turns an access failure into a false fact. Subagents should propagate structured failure context: type, attempted query, partial results.

eli5.question: When the payments system is down, the helper says “no previous refunds”. The clue is: the outages “usually last about an hour.” Waiting a few seconds won't fix it.
eli5.answer: If you phone a shop and nobody answers, you don't tell your friend “they have no stock”. You say “I couldn't get through”. The subagent must say “I couldn't check”, not “there's nothing”, and give what it tried and anything it did get. Then the coordinator can decide what to do. Rule: “couldn't look” and “looked and found nothing” must never look the same.
options: Runner-up. A quick retry then “unavailable” is decent, but hour-long outages beat the retries and the bare message hides the details.
Correct. Say it failed, what it tried, and what it got.
Saying “it failed, try later” is better than “nothing found”, but leaves out what was tried and what came back.
Moving the call to the coordinator doesn't change how a timeout gets reported.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the fix is to make the lookup succeed more often. That helps, but the dangerous part is the report: a timeout became “nothing found”, a false fact the coordinator acted on. Separating access failures from empty results is the guide's rule.

questions.question: Spoilage disputes can run long. When a chat nears the context limit, the SDK summarises older turns. Afterwards the agent sometimes offers a smaller credit than it promised earlier. It also forgets which items the customer listed. The tool results in these chats are short. Which change best fixes this?

options.t: Keep a running block of promised amounts, listed items and IDs, and put it at the top of every request.
options.why: Correct. Transactional facts kept outside the summarised history survive every summarisation pass, and placing them first keeps them prominent.

options.t: Trim each tool result to the few fields the agent uses before it is added to the conversation history.
options.why: Runner-up. Trimming is the fix when verbose tool output fills the context. These tool results are already short, so trimming saves little and the summaries still blur the promises.

options.t: Raise the context threshold at which older turns are summarised, keeping more of each chat verbatim.
options.why: Incorrect. This delays the loss rather than preventing it; long disputes still cross the threshold.

options.t: Ask the summariser to write longer summaries that quote every amount and item from the earlier turns.
options.why: Incorrect. A better summary prompt helps, but facts still pass through a lossy step each time. A separate facts block avoids that step.

questions.decider: The tool results are short and the loss comes from summarising turns that hold promises; if bulky tool output were filling the context, trimming results would compete.
questions.explanation: Progressive summarisation blurs numbers, dates and commitments. Extract them into a persistent case-facts block that is included in every request rather than summarised.

eli5.question: After long chats get squashed into a summary, the agent forgets what it promised. The clue is: “The tool results in these chats are short.” So the space isn't going on bulky tool output.
eli5.answer: A nurse at shift change doesn't rely on a retold story. They keep a chart on the bed: doses, times, allergies. The agent needs that chart (a case-facts block): promised amounts, items, IDs, sent at the top of every request. Summaries can blur; the chart doesn't. Rule: keep the numbers and promises in a fixed block, not in the summary.
options: Correct. A fixed list of the facts that travels with every request.
Runner-up. Cutting tool output down helps when tool output is the bulk. Here it is short.
Summarising later only delays the forgetting.
A better summary still squashes things; a separate fact list doesn't get squashed at all.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think context problems are always about size, so shrinking something is the fix. Here the issue is what summarisation does to exact facts: amounts and promises become vague. The fix is to keep those facts out of the summary path altogether.

questions.obj: 3.4 Plan mode for open design choices
questions.question: A ticket asks to replace the hand-written API client in mobile/ with one generated from the server's OpenAPI spec. Many screens call the old client. The team has not yet chosen between two generator libraries, and each one shapes the calls differently. How should the engineer start?

options.t: Work directly on one feature folder with the likelier library, run its tests, then roll the pattern out.
options.why: Runner-up. A direct spike plus tests suits a migration whose target is settled. With the library undecided, the spike bakes in a guess, and later folders follow it.

options.t: Use plan mode: have Claude survey call sites, compare both libraries and agree a design before edits.
options.why: Correct. An open choice with multi-file impact is what plan mode is for: explore and decide before committing to edits.

options.t: Send an Explore subagent to map the call sites and how each library would change them, then edit.
options.why: Incorrect. Exploring in a subagent keeps output out of the main context, but goes straight to edits with no agreed design.

options.t: Have Claude interview the engineer about the old client's edge cases, then make the change with direct edits.
options.why: Incorrect. Interviewing gathers requirements; the open question here is a design choice that needs the code surveyed.

questions.decider: The team has not chosen between two generators that shape calls differently; if the library were already chosen, incremental direct edits with tests would be fine.
questions.explanation: Plan mode fits large changes with multiple valid approaches or architectural decisions. Direct execution fits well-scoped changes whose approach is settled.

eli5.question: A big change across many screens, with a choice still open. The clue is: “The team has not yet chosen between two generator libraries.”
eli5.answer: You don't start knocking down walls before choosing between two floor plans. Plan mode is the drawing board: Claude looks around, compares the options and proposes a plan before touching code. Rule: open design choice or many files → plan first; settled and small → just do it.

Correct. Look, compare, decide, then edit.
A scout maps the ground, but nobody agrees a plan before the digging starts.
Questions about edge cases don't settle which library to use.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think small careful steps make any change safe. Steps and tests protect against breaking things, not against building on a choice that turns out wrong. With an unmade design decision, every early folder is a bet.

questions.question: A script runs claude -p to generate tests for each new endpoint. It then reads Claude's reply to learn which files were created and whether the tests passed. The wording changes from run to run, and the parser keeps breaking. The script needs named fields it can rely on. Which TWO changes fit best?

options.t: Add --output-format json to the command and read the result out of the JSON it prints.
options.why: Correct. JSON output gives the script a machine-readable envelope instead of free text.

options.t: Put a JSON example of the reply in the prompt and ask Claude to answer with only that JSON object.
options.why: Runner-up. A format example in the prompt usually gets the shape right and suits output a person reads. A parser needs the structure enforced by the CLI, not usually followed.

options.t: Supply a --json-schema defining a list of new files and a pass or fail field for the run.
options.why: Correct. The schema fixes which named fields the result contains. Together with JSON output, the script gets the fields it needs.

options.t: Add --verbose to the command and read the created files from the tool-call log it prints.
options.why: Incorrect. Verbose output is diagnostic text whose layout is not a contract; the script would parse a different free-text stream.

questions.decider: A script parses the output and needs reliable named fields; if a person read the reply, a format example in the prompt would be enough.
questions.explanation: For scripts, use the CLI's structured output: --output-format json for a machine-readable envelope and --json-schema for the fields. Prompt-level format requests remain probabilistic.

eli5.question: A script reads Claude's reply and breaks when the wording changes. The clue is: “The script needs named fields it can rely on.”
eli5.answer: A program reading a chatty letter will trip over it. Give it a filled-in form instead. --output-format json turns the reply into data; --json-schema says exactly which boxes the form has. You need both: one makes it a form, the other fixes the boxes. Rule: if a program reads it, ask for JSON with a schema.
options: Correct. Makes the reply machine-readable.
Runner-up. Showing a JSON sample usually works. A parser needs “every time”, which the CLI flags give.
Correct. Fixes the exact fields inside it.
The detailed log is meant for people debugging, not for programs to read.

questions.question: The /new-endpoint command describes the team's error-response format in prose. On simple endpoints Claude follows it. On endpoints with several failure cases, the error shapes differ from run to run. Claude can quote the prose rules when asked, so they are loading. What is the most effective change?

options.t: Rewrite the prose as a numbered checklist, one rule per failure case, stating the exact error JSON shape.
options.why: Incorrect. Sharper written rules help when rules are vague, but rules are already loaded and understood; output still varies on complex cases.

options.t: Add two or three complete handlers from the repo showing the error format across varied failures.
options.why: Correct. When instructions are loaded but output is still inconsistent, a few concrete examples are the most effective way to get consistent structure, especially on the hard cases.

options.t: Move the error rules into a .claude/rules/ file whose paths: glob matches the route handlers.
options.why: Runner-up. A path rule is the fix when conventions are not loading for the files being edited. Claude can quote these rules, so loading is not the problem.

options.t: Have a second, fresh Claude session review each generated endpoint against the error rules before it merges.
options.why: Incorrect. Independent review catches mistakes after generation; it does not make generation consistent.

questions.decider: Claude can quote the rules, so they are loaded but not applied consistently; if they were not loading for handler files, a path-scoped rule would be the fix.
questions.explanation: Few-shot examples are the most effective technique for consistent output when instructions alone are inconsistent. Pick examples that cover the hard cases.

eli5.question: Claude knows the error rules but applies them differently on complicated endpoints. The clue is: “Claude can quote the prose rules when asked, so they are loading.”
eli5.answer: A new cook who has read the recipe still plates differently each time. Show them three finished plates and they match. A few complete examples from the repo show the exact shape, including the tricky cases. Rule: rules loaded but output inconsistent → add a few good examples.
options: A tidier checklist is still instructions, and instructions alone are what vary on hard cases.
Correct. Show the shape with real examples that cover the hard cases.
Runner-up. A path rule fixes rules that don't load. These do load.
A reviewer catches mistakes afterwards; it doesn't stop them.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think inconsistent output means the instructions aren't reaching Claude. Here they are: Claude can quote them. The gap is between knowing a rule and applying it the same way on complex cases. Examples close that gap better than more prose.

questions.question: A /check-migration command asks Claude to “flag risky Prisma migrations”. It flags almost every migration, and engineers now skip its output. The team counts as risky only dropping a column, changing a column's type, or adding a required column with no default. Which change best improves precision?

options.t: Tell Claude to be conservative and to report a migration only when it is highly confident of a risk.
options.why: Incorrect. Confidence wording does not improve precision the way categorical criteria do.

options.t: Add several past migrations labelled risky or safe, each with a line explaining the verdict.
options.why: Runner-up. Labelled examples are the fix when the line is hard to state and ambiguous cases need demonstrating. Here the team can list the categories outright.

options.t: Name those operations as the flag criteria, each with a small migration snippet, and say other changes pass.
options.why: Correct. The team can state exactly what counts. Categorical criteria with concrete snippets replace the vague word “risky” and cut false positives.

options.t: Have Claude give each finding a severity score and show engineers only the findings scored high.
options.why: Incorrect. Without criteria, the scores are as vague as the flags; filtering them hides the problem.

questions.decider: The team can name exactly which operations count; if the boundary were fuzzy and hard to state, labelled examples would lead.
questions.explanation: Vague instructions like “risky” produce false positives that erode trust. Replace them with explicit categorical criteria, ideally with concrete examples of each.

eli5.question: A checker flags nearly everything as “risky”. The clue is: the team “counts as risky only” three specific operations. The rule can be written down exactly.
eli5.answer: Telling a guard “stop anyone suspicious” gets everyone stopped. Telling them “stop anyone without a badge” works. Write the three operations down as the explicit criteria, with a tiny example of each, and say everything else passes. Rule: if you can name what counts, name it; don't say “be careful”.
options: “Be careful” and “only if sure” don't sharpen what counts.
Runner-up. Labelled examples help when the line is hard to describe. Here it's easy to describe.
Correct. Name exactly what counts, with a small example each.
Scores on vague flags are still vague.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think examples are always the strongest prompt tool. They shine when a boundary is fuzzy. When the team can state the categories exactly, explicit criteria are the direct fix, and the guide says vague words like “risky” are what cause false positives.

questions.question: Midway through generating a set of screens, an engineer sees the context is nearly full. Most of it is long test output from earlier runs. Claude's recent answers are still accurate and refer to specific files. Nothing has changed in the repository outside this session. What should the engineer do next?

options.t: Have Claude write its decisions to a notes file, then open a new session that starts by reading that file.
options.why: Runner-up. A scratchpad plus a fresh session is right when answers have degraded or the work spans sessions. Here answers are still specific and the session is current.

options.t: Start routing future test runs through a subagent that returns only the failing tests and their causes.
options.why: Incorrect. Good for future runs, but it does not free the context that is already nearly full.

options.t: Resume the same session by name with --resume in a new terminal and continue from there.
options.why: Incorrect. Resuming reloads the same conversation, with the same full context.

options.t: Run /compact to condense the conversation so far, then carry on generating the remaining screens.
options.why: Correct. The session is healthy and current; only space is short. Compacting frees context while keeping the work in the same session.

questions.decider: Answers are still accurate and specific and nothing changed outside the session, so only space is short; if answers had turned vague or contradictory, a notes file and a fresh session would win.
questions.explanation: /compact reduces context usage within a session. Scratchpads and fresh sessions are for degradation or work that crosses session boundaries; subagents prevent future bloat.

eli5.question: The session is nearly full, mostly with old test logs, but Claude is still sharp. The clue is: “Claude's recent answers are still accurate and refer to specific files.”
eli5.answer: Your desk is covered in old printouts but you still know exactly what you're doing. Clear the desk and keep working; don't move to a new office. /compact squeezes the conversation so far and lets you carry on. Rule: healthy but full → /compact; confused or switching sessions → notes file and a fresh start.
options: Runner-up. Notes plus a fresh session fit when Claude has started to get vague. It hasn't.
Good habit for later runs, but the desk is already full now.
Resuming brings back the same full desk.
Correct. Free the space and keep going.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a full context always calls for a fresh session. A fresh session with notes is the remedy for degraded answers or work across sessions. When the session is still sharp and current, the lighter tool is /compact.

questions.question: An engineer pastes a long product spec into Claude to build a booking endpoint. The spec opens with an overview and ends with acceptance criteria. The generated code meets both. It misses rules from the middle sections, such as the late-cancellation window. Every section fits easily in the context. Which change best fixes this?

options.t: Put a short list of the key rules first in the prompt, with the full spec below under clear headings.
options.why: Correct. Models attend reliably to the start and end of long input and can miss the middle. Lifting the key rules to the top under clear headings counters that.

options.t: Split the spec by section, have Claude implement each in its own pass, then run one integration pass.
options.why: Runner-up. Per-section passes plus integration suit input too large for one context. The spec fits easily, and the miss is about position, not size.

options.t: Move the acceptance criteria to the top of the prompt, ahead of the overview and the rest of the spec.
options.why: Incorrect. Right idea, wrong content: the acceptance criteria are already honoured; the missed rules stay in the middle.

options.t: Have Claude summarise the spec first, then build the endpoint from that summary in place of the full text.
options.why: Incorrect. Summaries compress details like time windows; this risks losing the very rules being missed.

questions.decider: The missed rules sit in the middle of input that fits easily; if the spec were too large for one context, splitting it into passes would be the stronger choice.
questions.explanation: Long inputs suffer from “lost in the middle”: beginnings and ends are processed reliably, middles less so. Put key facts first and use explicit section headings.

eli5.question: Claude follows the start and end of a long spec but misses the middle. The clue is: “It misses rules from the middle sections.” And it all fits, so size isn't the issue.
eli5.answer: People remember the first and last items on a long list best. Models do too (lost in the middle). Pull the key rules to the top as a short list, then give the full spec with clear headings. Rule: put what matters first, and label the sections.
options: Correct. Key rules first, clear headings below.
Runner-up. Splitting helps when the input is too big or naturally separate. This fits and is one endpoint.
Moving things up is right, but these criteria were already followed. The missed rules are still buried.
A summary squashes exactly the small details being missed.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think missed requirements mean the input is too big, so it should be split. The pattern here is positional: start and end are honoured, the middle isn't, and it all fits. That is lost in the middle, fixed by layout.
